TASTE, SPEECH, TONGUE. [11] [Arg. n.]
Taste : sweetish bitter ; sour ; metallic, astringent ; inky ; lost.
Speech stammering. θ Typhus.
Cannot talk ; spasms of muscles of tongue and throat.
Tongue coated white ; yellow white.
Red, painful tip of tongue, papillæ erect, prominent.
Tongue dry, hard as a chip, and black like teeth. θ Typhus.
Red streak down middle of tongue.
Tongue dry, with thirst.
Glossitis.
Tongue white and moist (Pulsat. after Arg. nitr.)
Tongue furred with clean edges. θ Dyspepsia.
   

INNER MOUTH. [12] [Arg. n.]
Fetor from mouth ; morning.
Ptyalism.
Inner mouth covered with a whitish-grey coat.
Tough phlegm in mouth.
   

PALATE AND THROAT. [13] [Arg. n.]
Chronic angina.
Uvula and fauces dark red.
(OBS :) Chronic induration of tonsils.
Thick tenacious mucus in throat, obliging him to hawk ; causing slight hoarseness.
Rawness, soreness ; scraping in throat, causes hawking and cough.
Sensation as if a splinter was lodged in throat, when swallowing, eructating, breathing, stretching or moving neck.
Wart-like excrescences feel like pointed bodies when swallowing.
Felt as if he had a stick in throat when swallowing.
Sense as if throat was contracted, swallows with pain. θ Dyspepsia.
Swallowing difficult. θ Typhus.
Food feels as if lodged in throat. θ Dyspepsia.
Burning and dryness in fauces and pharynx.
Paroxysms of cramp in œsophagus.
   

APPETITE, THIRST. DESIRES, AVERSIONS. [14] [Arg. n.]
Appetite fair. θ Hypochondriasis.
Appetite sometimes fair enough, is generally very bad. θ Myopia.
Appetite good, but nearly all kinds of food distressed, whether abstemious or eating heartily. θ Hypochondriasis.
Appetite dulled by pain. θ Gastric ulcer.
Loss of appetite ; much thirst, or no thirst.
Refuses drink unless it is sweetened, yet thirsty.
Diminished appetite, frequent eructations, nausea with humming in ears. θ Locomotor ataxia.
Want of appetite. θ Melancholia.
Most fond of plum sauce, though swallowing was difficult. θ Typhus.
Irresistible desire for sugar.
Desire for strong cheese.
   

EATING AND DRINKING. [15] [Arg. n.]
Eating relieves squeamishness, but increases gastric pains.
Warm fluids relieve, cold aggravate, pains in stomach.
Eating, or a swallow of wine, relieves head ; coffee aggravates.
Sour things lessen nausea.
Pain immediately after eating. θ Dyspepsia.
Ten minutes after eating, flatulence. θ Dyspepsia.
Nausea after each meal, mostly after dinner.
Soon after taking food pain in stomach begins and continues so long as food remains down ; vomiting results about an hour after. θ Gastric ulcer.
Pains come on soon after eating, sometimes immediately on swallowing, as if œsophagus was irritated as much as stomach. θ Gastralgia.
Pain after every meal, half an hour after eating, epigastric, extending to left side. θ Dyspepsia.
Pain after eating, sometimes directly, sometimes an hour or more, with much belching and rumbling in bowels. θ Dyspepsia.
Pain after eating extends from pit of sternum to round along under heart, corresponding to situation of stomach. θ Gastric ulcer.
After a hearty meal, melancholia, especially after liquid food. θ Hypochondriasis.
By a very heavy meal, epileptiform convulsions are brought on.
After drinking, dyspnœa, drinks suffocate. θ Cholera.
Fluids go "right through him." θ Cholera infantum, etc.
